checkpoints: Identifies the root cause: merging two phases with opposite characteristics into one synchronous HTTP request — "accept the request" (tens of milliseconds, must not block) versus "do the heavy work" (seconds to minutes, CPU/IO-bound).
Explains that this merging violates the gateway's timeout budget as load grows, since the client/gateway can't wait minutes for a response meant to return in milliseconds.
Explains that a mid-transcode crash loses all progress because there is no checkpoint to resume from — the work has to restart from zero.
Explains that coupling ingestion and transcoding into one process prevents scaling each side independently based on its own distinct load profile.
States the core fix: on upload, insert a job row as PENDING and return HTTP 202 with the job id immediately, so the handler itself never blocks on the transcode.
States that a separate fire-and-forget worker performs the actual transcode in the background, moving the job through PROCESSING to either COMPLETED or FAILED.
States that the client's only interface is polling GET /jobs/:id repeatedly, and it only uses the result once status reaches COMPLETED.
Explains that the persisted job row is the single source of truth for status, so if the service restarts mid-job, that DB row — not in-memory worker state — is what recovery reads.
Adaptive bitrate is not "serve worse-quality video when the network is bad" — it is packaging ONE source video into several encodes (variants) declared in a manifest, plus independent segments.
A single static file cannot adapt: it makes a weak-network viewer buffer constantly or time out because the file is too heavy.
A strong-network viewer wastes headroom stuck at one fixed quality.
HLS solves this by cutting the video into fixed-length segments, each opening on a complete keyframe so it can serve as a valid starting point for playback.
HLS lists the variants in a master playlist by BANDWIDTH/RESOLUTION.
The player estimates throughput from the segment it just downloaded and picks the highest variant it can still keep up with — the server takes no part whatsoever in that decision.
That is exactly why the server stays stateless and CDN-friendly: each segment is an independent, cacheable HTTP GET.
The player can switch variant at any segment boundary.

Setting `s-maxage=31536000` with `immutable` tells shared caches to hold a response for a year and tells clients the URL will never return different content — a promise that only holds when a URL is permanently bound to one piece of content, such as a content-addressed or versioned asset key.

A live playlist's payload mutates in place under the same key, so applying the static-asset directive to it means the edge caches the first response and keeps serving that same stale segment list to every viewer at that PoP for up to a year, with no natural mechanism to pick up the update.

The correct caching strategy for frequently-changing dynamic content is a short edge TTL such as `s-maxage=10` combined with `stale-while-revalidate`, which keeps the cache close to live state while absorbing revalidation cost without blocking clients.

Long-TTL `immutable` caching belongs exclusively to static, versioned assets whose URL changes whenever the underlying content changes — never to a key whose payload can change while the URL itself stays fixed.

When a handler throws an exception such as `NotFoundException` instead of returning an explicit response, the resulting error status carries no `Cache-Control` header of its own, leaving a shared cache free to apply its own default caching policy to that response.

Caching an unknown-key 404 turns a transient miss — a key not yet propagated from an upload pipeline, or momentarily absent mid-migration — into a sticky failure, since every viewer routed through that cache during the caching window keeps seeing 'not found' long after the origin would correctly serve the content.

The origin should answer unknown keys with a non-throwing 200-style fallback carrying an explicit short-TTL or `no-store` Cache-Control, giving the edge a deliberate, bounded instruction rather than leaving the outcome to a shared cache's default handling of an uncontrolled error status.

Locking this class of bug down in tests requires asserting the exact `Cache-Control` string per asset type — not just header presence — plus a separate test confirming an unknown key returns a bounded, non-cached response rather than being cached as a hard error.

`ensureTranscoded` guards against re-running the encode with a single check — whether `manifest.m3u8` already exists on disk — and nothing else; there is no lock or claim placed on a `videoId` before the ladder starts.

Because the existence check and the encode work are not atomic, every concurrent request for the same cold video (a `POST encode` call and several first `manifest.m3u8` fetches arriving together) sees the file missing at the same instant and independently starts the full three-rung FFmpeg ladder, multiplying CPU by the number of simultaneous requests instead of costing one ladder per video.

With no in-flight lock, these parallel ladders also race to write the same output files (segments and the master playlist), so whichever run finishes last wins and the others' encoding work is wasted or can corrupt the result.

The fix is coalescing concurrent callers onto a single run rather than adding a bigger lock around the whole method: keep an in-flight `Map<string, Promise<void>>` on the service, and once the existence check misses, look the `videoId` up in that map before starting any work.

If a promise for that `videoId` is already in the map, the caller awaits it and returns instead of starting a second run; if not, the caller starts the encode, stores its promise in the map synchronously before the first `await` so a concurrent caller sees it immediately, and removes the entry in a `finally` once the run settles.
This coalescing pattern is the same shape as request-deduping or dataloader batching, just keyed by `videoId` — it turns N concurrent first-requests for a cold video into exactly one FFmpeg run.

An in-memory map only protects a single process; if encoding must be durable across multiple server instances, `ensureTranscoded` needs to move onto a job queue (e.g. BullMQ) keyed by `videoId`, so a second instance also awaits the existing job instead of starting its own.

Lazy transcoding is the right default for a library where most uploads are never watched, since it avoids spending CPU on clips nobody opens, but it forces the first viewer of any video to wait out the full ladder before their manifest resolves.
Eager pre-encoding on upload makes the first play instant because the ladder already ran, but it burns CPU and storage transcoding effectively all uploads, most of which are never watched.

A reasonable middle ground is to eager-encode only content with an existing signal of being hot (an established creator, a flagged launch) and keep the lock-protected lazy path as the fallback for the long tail of uploads.

The metric that proves the coalescing fix worked is the count of concurrent FFmpeg processes, or `ensureTranscoded` calls that actually reach the encode loop rather than hitting the map and awaiting, per cold `videoId` — this scales with request concurrency before the fix and is pinned at exactly 1 after it.

A test that fires many concurrent `POST encode` calls for one fresh video id and asserts exactly one FFmpeg run occurred, producing one clean (non-corrupted) manifest, demonstrates the fix rather than just plausibly describing it.

When a proxy cache key is built from the full request URI, marketing query parameters like utm_source and utm_campaign become part of the key, so every share link to the same asset produces a distinct cache entry for identical bytes — this is cache pollution, and it prevents requests that should HIT from ever coalescing.

A Vary: Cookie header applied to every response, including public and non-personalized assets, makes the cache store one entry per session cookie instead of one shared entry per URI — an unbounded explosion that has nothing to do with the actual response bytes.

Vary: Accept-Encoding is only safe when it reflects a small canonical set of encodings (e.g. gzip, br, identity); varying on the raw, unnormalized Accept-Encoding header value fragments the cache into more entries than the number of distinct response bodies actually requires.

The fix for query-string pollution is to normalize the cache key: strip parameters that don't affect the response body (such as utm_* tracking params) and canonicalize the order of whatever parameters remain, so equivalent requests collapse onto the same entry.

Middleware that blanket-sets Vary: Cookie for session-aware responses must be scoped to only the routes whose output genuinely differs per user; it must never run in front of public, session-independent routes such as a CDN content/:key endpoint.

A falling HIT ratio paired with rising origin load points to a mismatch between the cache-key/Vary configuration and what actually changes the response, not to cache size or network/TLS problems — that mismatch is what forces otherwise-identical requests to MISS and fall through to origin.

Confirming a cache-key and Vary fix means watching the HIT ratio and the X-Cache-Status distribution climb back toward their pre-regression levels, and adding an alert on the HIT ratio so a future key or Vary regression is caught by the metric instead of discovered through an origin-load incident.

The states are PENDING → PROCESSING → COMPLETED | FAILED, persisted server-side in the job row as the single source of truth — not derived from a queue, a worker's memory, or the caller's belief about what happened; if the service restarts mid-job, the row is exactly what recovery reads.
Transitions are constrained, not free-form: a job only moves to COMPLETED after the artifact has genuinely been uploaded to storage.
FAILED always carries a populated errorMessage so the caller knows why.
outputPath/outputUrl are meaningful only in the COMPLETED state — they stay null everywhere else, by contract, not by convention.

The GET /jobs/:id response is designed around one rule: the client branches on status, full stop — it must never infer completion from a non-null outputPath, because that couples the poll loop to an implementation detail that could change.

The response also has to distinguish two different "no" answers cleanly: a job that exists but ended badly (status: FAILED, HTTP 200, with errorMessage) versus a job that was never created at all (HTTP 404) — collapsing both into one soft-200 shape hides a real error from monitoring and from the client.

A contract this small should name exactly one honest extension point rather than pretend to be finished forever — most commonly a stuck-PROCESSING recovery sweep (a startup or scheduled query for jobs stuck past a timeout that moves them to FAILED or re-enqueues them) or an explicit retry transition back to PENDING.

That extension is designed in as a named transition on the same state machine, not bolted on as a side channel — and the contract stops there instead of speculatively adding states for cases that have not actually happened yet.
States the ladder (array of rungs) is the single source of truth — both the FFmpeg encode config and the HLS manifest are derived from it, never hand-authored separately.
Names the rung's contract as exactly: a label (doubling as the variant sub-path, e.g. `720p/`), width, height, a bandwidth in bits/s, and the relative variant-playlist URI.
States width/height map straight to the manifest's `RESOLUTION` attribute and bandwidth maps to the advertised `BANDWIDTH` attribute.

Describes the builder as purely mechanical: walk the ladder in order and, per rung, emit one `#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=...,RESOLUTION=...` line followed by that rung's URI — the manifest is generated output, never hand-edited.
States that adding a new rung (e.g. 1440p) is just appending one entry (label/width/height/bandwidth/URI) to the ladder array, and the builder picks it up on the next manifest write.

States the player needs zero code changes because it was never coded against a fixed quality list — it is purely `BANDWIDTH`-driven, comparing measured throughput against whatever `BANDWIDTH` values appear in the manifest it just fetched.

States the ordering/spacing validity rule: rungs must be ascending by `BANDWIDTH` with roughly a ~2x gap between neighbors, and explains why (too small a gap → player can't reliably distinguish rungs, causing thrash or no switching; too large a gap → a switch becomes a jarring visible jump).

`max-age` only caches inside each user's own browser, so it does nothing for a flash crowd of tens of thousands of distinct users - each browser cache is its own private store, isolated from every other browser.

50,000 first requests from 50,000 distinct users are still 50,000 origin hits because there is no shared store between them - this is exactly why the origin stays overloaded despite `max-age` being set on every response.
The fix is a shared cache layer at the edge - a proxy / CDN PoP near the users - sitting in front of the origin.

At that shared edge layer, the first request at a PoP is a `MISS` that goes upstream, and every subsequent request at that same PoP is a `HIT` served locally, absorbing the spike and cutting both latency and origin load.
The header that makes the edge hold the copy is `s-maxage` (the shared-cache TTL), completely independent of the browser's own `max-age`.

You observe it by the `X-Cache-Status` header flipping from `MISS` to `HIT` when the same asset is fetched twice through the edge - and its total absence when calling the origin directly, proving the cache is really at the edge, not the origin.
On the second call, `createJob` queries for an existing job with the same `inputPath` and `status != FAILED`.
It finds the job created just before the timeout and returns it - same `id`, no new row created.
Because no new row is created, no second FFmpeg process gets spawned.
That's exactly what makes `POST` idempotent under network retries and accidental double-submits: one `inputPath` always resolves to one job regardless of how many times it's called.

The guard's coverage has exactly one gap that backfires: a job stuck at `PROCESSING` (worker crashed after setting `PROCESSING` but before the transcode finished) blocks every re-trigger indefinitely, because it's neither `FAILED` nor genuinely still progressing.
The complete design pairs this idempotency guard with a stuck-job detector - a startup or periodic routine that marks `PROCESSING` jobs older than a threshold as `FAILED` or re-enqueues them.
Segment duration trades ABR reaction speed against request/playlist overhead - there is no single number that is free of trade-offs.
Short segments (around 2 seconds) let the player re-measure throughput and switch variant almost immediately, recovering fast from a bandwidth drop.
But short segments multiply HTTP requests and playlist-refresh churn, adding per-request overhead all the way to the CDN.

Long segments (around 10 seconds) minimize request count and overhead but react slowly to network changes, and raise startup/seek latency because a full segment has to buffer before playback can begin.

Commit to concrete defaults instead of "it depends": live / low-latency streaming leans short (2-4 seconds) to keep both latency and reaction time tight, while VOD leans toward the common ~6-second default because it can tolerate slower reaction in exchange for efficiency - a deliberate point on the trade-off curve, not hand-waving.

Underneath both choices sits one constraint that bounds how far you can push: every segment must start on a complete keyframe, so segment length is bounded below by the encoder's own keyframe interval (GOP) - you cannot shrink segments past that floor without re-encoding the source.
